transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Doctor. I... well, I suppose I came because the folks over at my church have been getting a little worried about me, and to be honest, I'm a little confused by it all myself. I've been going to the same church for, oh, it must be near forty years now, and I always help out with the fellowship hour. We do these potlucks down in the basement, you know, where everyone brings a hot dish and we all sit together. I've always been the one to set up the tables, it's just my way of contributing since I don't work anymore. 

But lately, I keep doing these... well, just odd things. I don't rightly know how to explain it. Like just last Sunday, I was standing right there by the potluck table, and I had the big serving spoon for the potato salad, and I just... I held it up in the air and I didn't move. I just stood there frozen, holding that spoon up, and my mind was just blank. 

And it's not just the spoon. Another time, just a few weeks back, I was supposed to be setting out the paper goods. We use those nice thick paper napkins, you know? And I just kept folding the exact same stack of napkins. Just folding them over and over and over again, pressing the edges down real sharp. I didn't even realize what I was doing until I looked up and saw that a whole line of people was just standing there waiting on me to finish so they could get their plates and eat. Pastor Jim had to come over and gently take the napkins out of my hands. I've always been a good, quick helper, so I just don't understand why I'm doing these things and holding up the line.
When you were doing those repeated actions, did you feel driven to do them because of a fear or worry that something bad would happen if you didn’t?

Oh, heavens no. No, it wasn't like that at all. I wasn't scared of anything. You know, sometimes folks get all worked up down there thinking the casseroles will run out—especially when Mary Higgins brings her green bean bake, because everybody always wants a big scoop of that—but I wasn't worried about the food running out, and I certainly wasn't worried that something terrible was going to happen if I didn't fold those napkins just right. Lord knows the church has stood for a hundred years without my help. 

It wasn't a worry in my heart, Doctor, not a bit of fear. It's more like... well, it's like my brain just went on a little vacation without telling me. I didn't have a single thought in my head about trying to prevent something bad. I was just... folding. Just folding and folding. I remember I was looking at the little pressed flowers on the corners of those napkins—Pastor Jim gets them in bulk from the Sam's Club, you know, the nice thick ones because the cheap paper ones just fall apart the second they touch a dollop of potato salad—and I was just pressing that edge down. Pressing and pressing. 

There was no fear at all, just... quiet. Just my hands moving on their own while my mind was completely empty. So no, I wasn't trying to stop anything bad from happening. I just couldn't seem to stop myself from doing it.
When these repeated actions start, are you able to stop yourself if you try?

Well, that's the strange part of it, Doctor. I... I don't really try to stop, because I don't rightly know I'm doing it until someone points it out or until a good long while has passed. Like with the napkins, I didn't even have the thought cross my mind to stop folding them. It wasn't like I was sitting there thinking, "Oh, Beatrice, you've folded this napkin three times now, that's enough, time to move on to the next one." My mind just wasn't there to give the order to stop, if that makes any sense. 

I suppose if I realized what was happening in the moment, I might be able to put the napkin down or lower my arm with the spoon. But I just get so... stuck. It's like a needle skipping on one of those old record players my late husband used to listen to—he loved his Johnny Cash records, played them every Sunday afternoon after church, and sometimes the needle would catch on a speck of dust and just play the same little bit of a song over and over. That's what my hands do. They just catch on a speck of dust and keep going. 

And by the time Pastor Jim came over to take the napkins, I didn't fight him on it. I didn't feel like I *had* to keep folding them, so when he gently pulled them away, my hands just sort of dropped to my sides. But on my own? Without Pastor Jim or somebody tapping me on the shoulder to snap me out of it? I just don't know. I haven't really had the chance to try and stop myself, because I'm just not aware enough to even try. It's just so baffling, Doctor, really it is.
Do you remember what you were doing during these episodes, or is there a gap in your memory afterward?

Well, now, that's a... a very good question, Doctor. A very good question indeed. You see, it's not like I black out or anything like that. It's not like those stories you hear about folks waking up in a different town and not knowing how they got there. My sister-in-law, Martha—bless her heart, she passed about five years ago now—she used to have these spells where she'd just lose whole afternoons, but that was because of her blood sugar, you see. She had the terrible diabetes and wouldn't stay away from the pecan pie at the bake sales. But for me, it's nothing like Martha's spells. 

I don't have a gap in my memory, exactly. I know I was standing there. I know I was in the church basement, and I know I had the napkins or the serving spoon in my hand. It's just... well, it's like I remember it happening, but I remember it like I was watching somebody else do it, or like I was looking through a very thick piece of glass. I remember seeing my hands moving, folding that thick paper—and like I said, those Sam's Club napkins have those little pressed flowers on the edges, and I remember staring at those little flowers so hard. I remember the smell of Mary Higgins' green bean bake, and I remember hearing the chatter of the folks waiting in line. I remember all of that. 

So the memory is there, clear as day. It's just that during the time it's happening, there's no... no *me* driving the car, so to speak. I remember the folding, I remember the standing frozen with the spoon, but I don't remember having a single thought about it while it was going on. It's only afterward, when Pastor Jim takes the napkins or when I finally put the spoon down, that I think, "Well, Beatrice, what in the world were you just doing?" But the memory of doing it? Oh yes, I have that. I remember it all, it's just so terribly confusing to remember doing something that you didn't even realize you were doing at the time, if you understand what I mean.
During these episodes, do you ever lose awareness or consciousness, even briefly?

Oh, goodness gracious, no. No, no, I don't pass out or anything frightful like that. I've never been one to swoon, Doctor. You know, some folks get a little lightheaded when they're on their feet too long—like Mrs. Gable, she passed out cold during the Easter sunrise service a few years back. Just went right over into the azalea bushes! But to be fair, it was terribly muggy that morning and she had her good wool coat on, bless her heart, so we had to fan her with the church bulletins until she came to. 

But me? No, nothing like that at all. I'm awake the whole entire time. My eyes are wide open, and I'm standing right there on my own two feet. I don't slump over or get dizzy or go to sleep. Like I was saying before, I can hear everybody talking in the fellowship hall and I can smell the food... I'm just standing there. I don't lose my consciousness even for a second. 

I've always had a very strong constitution, you see. Never even fainted when I was having my babies, and my youngest, Thomas, was nearly nine pounds! The nurses couldn't believe it. So, no, I don't black out or lose awareness of the room. I'm right there. I know exactly where I am and what's going on around me. It's just... well, like I said, it's just my hands doing the moving while my mind is taking a rest, but I'm definitely fully awake for it.
Do you ever have sudden, brief jerking movements or twitches that seem to happen on their own?

Well, no, not... not like a twitch, Doctor. I know what you mean, like when your eye goes to jumping when you're tired? My husband used to get that terribly when he worked the late shift at the plant. His left eye would just flutter and jump like a moth at a porch light, and he'd say, "Bea, I think I need a cup of coffee and a good long nap." But no, I don't get anything like that. 

And it's certainly not like those big jerks, either. You know, like when you're just falling asleep in your armchair and suddenly your whole leg kicks out and wakes you right up? I do that sometimes when I'm watching my evening programs—usually right in the middle of Jeopardy!, wouldn't you know it, right when Alex Trebek... well, I suppose it's not Alex anymore, is it? May he rest in peace. But right when they're giving the Final Jeopardy clue, I'll nod off for just a second and—boom!—my leg kicks the coffee table and I spill my tea. 

But during the daytime? When I'm standing there at the church or in my kitchen? No, I don't have any sudden twitches or jerks. My hands don't jump around on their own. When they're folding those napkins or holding that spoon, they're moving smooth and steady, just... over and over. It's not a twitch at all. It's a very deliberate sort of movement, even if I'm not the one deliberating it, if that makes sense. So, no sudden jerking, thank goodness. I'd probably drop Mary Higgins' green bean bake right on the linoleum if I started jerking around like that!
When you are holding still like that, do you find yourself in a fixed posture that you can maintain for a long time, almost like your body is stuck in that position?

Well, yes... yes, that is exactly the word for it, Doctor. Stuck. It is exactly why I finally decided I needed to come in and see you, because it's just getting to be too much. I keep doing these odd things at church, and it really does feel just like my body is stuck in one position. 

Like I was telling you before about the potluck table. I'll be standing right there by the casseroles, and I'll pick up the serving spoon—and these aren't those flimsy plastic spoons, mind you, these are the heavy stainless steel ones we got from the restaurant supply store over in Greenville years and years ago, very sturdy—and I'll just hold it right up in the air. And I won't move a single muscle. I just stay frozen in that exact posture for the longest time. 

You’d think my arm would get terribly tired, wouldn't you? A seventy-one-year-old woman holding her arm up like that for goodness knows how long. But it doesn't. I'm just fixed there like a statue in the park. And the worst part is, there is a whole line of people right behind me, just waiting with their paper plates! The choir director, the Sunday school teachers... all of them just waiting on me to serve myself so they can get to the food, and I'm just standing there holding the spoon up to the ceiling. 

And if I'm not stuck holding the spoon, it's the napkins. I know I mentioned them already, but it's the exact same kind of stuck. I'll be standing there at the end of the buffet line, folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over and over again. Not moving my feet, not turning my head, just fixed in that one spot doing that one odd thing while everybody is waiting on me to hand them one so they can go sit down and eat. It's just... well, it's terribly embarrassing is what it is. It's why I'm here, Doctor. Because getting stuck like a rusty gear in front of the whole congregation is just not a normal thing to be doing, is it?
When you get stuck like that, if someone asks you to move or change position, do you feel unable to do it even if you want to?

Well, that's just the thing, Doctor, that's exactly the heart of the matter. When I'm standing there, holding that serving spoon up in the air by the casseroles, or when I'm just fixed in place folding those same paper napkins over and over... it's not that I don't want to move. I hear them. I hear Pastor Miller clear his throat behind me, or I hear little Susie tugging on her mother's dress saying she's hungry. I know they're waiting on me. 

And in my mind, I'm saying, "Bea, put the spoon down, Bea, hand the lady a napkin, for goodness sake, you're holding up the entire fellowship hall." But my body... it just won't listen. It's like my arms and legs belong to somebody else entirely, or like the connection between my brain and my muscles just went right ahead and took a vacation without telling me. 

Last Sunday, Margaret—Margaret Higgins, she's the one who always brings that lovely green bean bake I was telling you about, she's been bringing it since 1982, always uses the crispy onions on top, never the store-brand ones either—well, Margaret tapped me right on the shoulder. Very gently, you know, because she's a sweet woman, she really is, always the first to send a card if you're under the weather. She tapped me and she said, "Bea, honey, are you going to dish out some of those scalloped potatoes?" 

And I wanted to say yes! I wanted to just scoop them up and put them on my plate and keep walking down the line like a normal person. But I couldn't. I just stood there with the spoon up in the air, not moving an inch, not even turning my head to look at her. I felt just awful about it, I really did. I felt like a foolish old woman, making everyone wait while I do these odd things. It's just so strange, Doctor, wanting to move, knowing you *should* move, being asked to move... and just being completely unable to do it. It's why I'm here, because I just can't keep doing this at church, I just can't.
Do you ever hear voices or other sounds that other people around you do not hear?

Voices? Oh, goodness no. No, nothing like that at all. If anything, Doctor, my hearing is going in the exact opposite direction. I'm seventy-one years old, you know, and my ears just aren't what they used to be when I was a young girl working out on my daddy's farm. Back then, I swear I could hear a tractor coming from two miles down the county road, long before you could even see the dust kicking up. 

But these days? I have to sit right there in the second row at church just to hear Pastor Miller's sermons properly. And he uses a microphone! It's one of those fancy little ones that clips right onto his lapel. The church bought it with the bake sale money about three years ago because the old stand-up microphone kept making this awful screeching sound—you know, that high-pitched feedback? Just terrible. It would make your fillings ache, it really would. 

But to answer your question, no, I don't hear anything that isn't really there. I don't hear people whispering to me when the room is empty, or any strange noises. Now, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she swears up and down she hears her late husband walking around upstairs sometimes, just the floorboards creaking and his heavy work boots thumping around. But I always tell her, "Martha, it's just that old house settling." Old houses do that, you know, especially in the wintertime when the cold air makes the wood shrink up. 

But me? No, I don't get any of that. When I'm stuck there holding that serving spoon or folding those napkins, my mind is just as quiet as a mouse. Well, except for my own self telling my own body to move, like I was just explaining to you. But no outside voices, and no sounds that nobody else can hear. Just the regular church chatter, the choir practicing down the hall, and the clinking of the paper plates. So you don't have to worry about that with me. My ears might be getting a little dull with age, but they certainly aren't playing any tricks on me!

I'll be standing right there by the casseroles, and I'll pick up the serving spoon—and these aren't those flimsy plastic spoons, mind you, these are the heavy stainless steel ones we got from the restaurant supply store over in Greenville years and years ago, very sturdy—and I'll just hold it right up in the air. And I won't move a single muscle. I just stay frozen in that exact posture for the longest time. 

You’d think my arm would get terribly tired, wouldn't you? A seventy-one-year-old woman holding her arm up like that for goodness knows how long. But it doesn't. I'm just fixed there like a statue in the park. And the worst part is, there is a whole line of people right behind me, just waiting with their paper plates! The choir director, the Sunday school teachers... all of them just waiting on me to serve myself so they can get to the food, and I'm just standing there holding the spoon up to the ceiling. 

And if I'm not stuck holding the spoon, it's the napkins. I know I mentioned them already, but it's the exact same kind of stuck. I'll be standing there at the end of the buffet line, folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over and over again. Not moving my feet, not turning my head, just fixed in that one spot doing that one odd thing while everybody is waiting on me to hand them one so they can go sit down and eat. It's just... well, it's terribly embarrassing is what it is. It's why I'm here, Doctor. Because getting stuck like a rusty gear in front of the whole congregation is just not a normal thing to be doing, is it?

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed postures are accompanied by true loss of voluntary movement/negativism consistent with catatonia, rather than a dissociative state or compulsive ritual
doctor.question: When you get stuck like that, if someone asks you to move or change position, do you feel unable to do it even if you want to?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: Doctor, I came because at church I keep doing odd things, like standing by the potluck table holding the serving spoon up and not moving, or folding the same stack of napkins over and over while people are waiting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question about the patient's motor control and 'stuck' behavior, which directly relates to her disorganized/abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Well, that's just the thing, Doctor, that's exactly the heart of the matter. When I'm standing there, holding that serving spoon up in the air by the casseroles, or when I'm just fixed in place folding those same paper napkins over and over... it's not that I don't want to move. I hear them. I hear Pastor Miller clear his throat behind me, or I hear little Susie tugging on her mother's dress saying she's hungry. I know they're waiting on me. 

And in my mind, I'm saying, "Bea, put the spoon down, Bea, hand the lady a napkin, for goodness sake, you're holding up the entire fellowship hall." But my body... it just won't listen. It's like my arms and legs belong to somebody else entirely, or like the connection between my brain and my muscles just went right ahead and took a vacation without telling me. 

Last Sunday, Margaret—Margaret Higgins, she's the one who always brings that lovely green bean bake I was telling you about, she's been bringing it since 1982, always uses the crispy onions on top, never the store-brand ones either—well, Margaret tapped me right on the shoulder. Very gently, you know, because she's a sweet woman, she really is, always the first to send a card if you're under the weather. She tapped me and she said, "Bea, honey, are you going to dish out some of those scalloped potatoes?" 

And I wanted to say yes! I wanted to just scoop them up and put them on my plate and keep walking down the line like a normal person. But I couldn't. I just stood there with the spoon up in the air, not moving an inch, not even turning my head to look at her. I felt just awful about it, I really did. I felt like a foolish old woman, making everyone wait while I do these odd things. It's just so strange, Doctor, wanting to move, knowing you *should* move, being asked to move... and just being completely unable to do it. It's why I'm here, because I just can't keep doing this at church, I just can't.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there are persistent non-motor psychotic symptoms, especially auditory hallucinations, to distinguish catatonia in schizophrenia from conversion/dissociative or obsessive-compulsive phenomena.
doctor.question: Do you ever hear voices or other sounds that other people around you do not hear?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices or sounds), but my symptom profile does not include any symptoms related to hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Voices? Oh, goodness no. No, nothing like that at all. If anything, Doctor, my hearing is going in the exact opposite direction. I'm seventy-one years old, you know, and my ears just aren't what they used to be when I was a young girl working out on my daddy's farm. Back then, I swear I could hear a tractor coming from two miles down the county road, long before you could even see the dust kicking up. 

But these days? I have to sit right there in the second row at church just to hear Pastor Miller's sermons properly. And he uses a microphone! It's one of those fancy little ones that clips right onto his lapel. The church bought it with the bake sale money about three years ago because the old stand-up microphone kept making this awful screeching sound—you know, that high-pitched feedback? Just terrible. It would make your fillings ache, it really would. 

But to answer your question, no, I don't hear anything that isn't really there. I don't hear people whispering to me when the room is empty, or any strange noises. Now, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she swears up and down she hears her late husband walking around upstairs sometimes, just the floorboards creaking and his heavy work boots thumping around. But I always tell her, "Martha, it's just that old house settling." Old houses do that, you know, especially in the wintertime when the cold air makes the wood shrink up. 

But me? No, I don't get any of that. When I'm stuck there holding that serving spoon or folding those napkins, my mind is just as quiet as a mouse. Well, except for my own self telling my own body to move, like I was just explaining to you. But no outside voices, and no sounds that nobody else can hear. Just the regular church chatter, the choir practicing down the hall, and the clinking of the paper plates. So you don't have to worry about that with me. My ears might be getting a little dull with age, but they certainly aren't playing any tricks on me!

inference.note: This presentation strongly supports dissociative stupor: episodes of immobility with preserved awareness and no hallucinations, seizures, or true compulsive fear-driven rituals. Catatonic schizophrenia (F20.2) and mixed obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2) are less consistent with the absence of psychosis, obsessions, or compulsions driven by anxiety.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview most strongly supports dissociative stupor/catatonic-like episodes with preserved consciousness: the patient has repeated episodes of motor immobility or fixed posture (holding a spoon up, standing frozen), diminished voluntary control over movement, and a subjective sense that her mind goes blank while she remains awake and aware. She denies fear-driven compulsions, loss of consciousness, amnesia, hallucinations, or jerking/tic-like movements. The presentation best fits F44.2 among the provided candidate set.
